subject: Parameter values not being sampled - Multi species N Mixture Model

messages.author: e0fddb5311ed7959
messages.subject: Parameter values not being sampled - Multi species N Mixture Model
parts:
Hi All, 
I have been working on a modified version of the multi species binomial n-mixture model from AHM Vol2. I am running into a strange issue where some N values for one particular species (roughly 50% of sites detected) are stuck at the Initial Values and appear not to have been sampled (i.e. estimates are the initial values, trace plots are flat, and the effective sample size is 0), no matter how many iterations I run the MCMC for. 

I have tried many combinations of Initial Values, and tried both JAGS and Nimble, so I'm confident there's something specific about this species that the model is running into issues for. But I can't work out what it is. All other species seem fine and the N values are reasonable. This species is the most commonly detected species. 

This is a much simplified version of my model with the issue here: 
model_code = nimbleCode({
  # Priors
  # Intercepts and coefficients all fixed effects
  for(k in 1:nspec){
    mean.lambda[k] <- exp(beta0[k])
    beta0[k] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
    alpha0[k] <- logit(mean.p[k])
    alpha1[k] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
    mean.p[k] ~ dunif(0,1)
    beta1[k] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  }
  # Specify MVN prior for random site effects in lambda for each species
  for (i in 1:nsites){
    eta.lam[i,1:nspec] ~ dmnorm(mu.eta[1:nspec], Omega[,])
  }
  for (k in 1:nspec){
    mu.eta[k] <- 0
  }
  # Vague inverse Wishart prior for variance-covariance matrix
  Omega[1:nspec,1:nspec] ~ dwish(R[,], df)
  Sigma2[1:nspec,1:nspec] <- inverse(Omega[,])
 
  # Scale var/covar matrix to become the correlation matrix
  for (i in 1:nspec){
    for (k in 1:nspec){
      rho[i,k] <- Sigma2[i,k] / (sqrt(Sigma2[i,i]) * sqrt(Sigma2[k,k]))
    }
  }
  # Likelihood
  # Ecological model for true abundance
  for (i in 1:nsites){
    for(k in 1:nspec){
      N[i,k] ~ dpois(lambda[i,k])
      log(lambda[i,k]) <- beta0[k] +
        beta1[k] * rainfall[i] +
        eta.lam[i,k]
     
      # Observation model for replicated counts
      for (j in 1:nreps){
        C[i,j,k] ~ dbin(p[i,j,k], N[i,k])
        logit(p[i,j,k]) <- alpha0[k] + alpha1[k]*date[i]
      }
    }
  }})

If anyone has any suggestions I would be very appreciative. I have attached a reproducible example of the code and data if anyone has time to play around with it. 

Thanks heaps,
Billy

messages.author: af31ce3a70c4aa9e
messages.subject: Re: Parameter values not being sampled - Multi species N Mixture Model
parts:
Hi Billy,

I spent a bit of time working through your code, I suspect this is a data management issue, although I can't really pin it down from here. There is one major issue that jumped out:
Your data are all either 1s or 0s, but this is written as an N-mixture model. The data (y, or 'C' in the model) should be counts, not detection/non-detections. I'm not sure how well you can estimate variation in abundance if your data are just 1's and 0's. There is a class of models known as  N-occupancy models (developed by Rossman and Zipkin following ideas from Royle and Nichols) that attempts to do this. I think they're challenging to fit (particularly if many species are almost never detected, with the exception of Woylie it seems you detect most species ~ once or twice every 100 surveys?), and the models are written slightly differently? Perhaps this was an issue on the back end and these should be integers from 0 to some number bigger than 1?

Because of this, I don't think you're 'stuck on your initial values.' If you look at the estimates of detection the p for the only common species is ~0.3. You detect it about 30% of the time. If you have a ton of data that look like this: y = [1,0,1,0,1, ... ,1,0,0,0,1], and you use this model
y ~ binomial(N, p)
You will get an estimate that N really is 1 (which is being interpreted as stuck, but is your actual estimate), because the detection probability is high enough that you should have at least one '2' or '3' (or '7') in your data if the data are truly binomially distributed and N is greater than 1.

Please note that N-mixture models can also struggle to fit data like this (0s 99% of the time). You might be better off with zero-inflated Poisson regression (assuming you have counts and not detection/non-detection data) or something similar.

There are a couple of other issues I bumped into:
1) 'covs' isn't in the RData or clearly defined in the script. I assumed it was in the Site information in 'dethist.' No big deal on your end, but hampers quick answers.
2) inverse-Wishart priors are the conjugate prior for a multivariate normal covariance matrix, but that doesn't mean they're 'vague'. Alvarez (2014, Iowa State) wrote a great thesis about this. Barnard et al. (2000; Statistica Sinica) wrote a more complex but also wonderful paper that I think motivated Alvarez's work. There is some other interesting work on scaling Wishart priors, but I view these as kind of 'hacks' to try to get away from inverse-Wishart problems, as opposed to what Barnard and Alvarez propose. This has mainly been identified as a problem with the logit-link for 'Ecological' analyses, but I suspect it could cause problems with any link-function. See Fay et al. (2021, MEE) for a more ecology focused example of how this can cause problems. There are some great ways to deal with this in Nimble and Stan by decomposing the covariance matrix into components, and putting priors on the components. Lots of posts on here about that. Fay et al. also have a solution that works fairly well in JAGS.

Best wishes! hmecology might also be a great place to post this kind of stuff.

Thomas
